From the St. Thomas Times, August 4, 1847 COLONIAL LIFE ASSURANCE COM- PANY. We take leave to refer our readers to a notice which appears in our advertising columns, announcing that ihe above company will ellect assurances on the lives of persons residing in these islands on reasonable terms, and referring for every information that can he required to John Morrison Jr. Esq., Merchant of this city and Agent to the company. The principles on which lives can with safety he assured, have been understood and acted on in Europe for upwards of a century, but it is only vvithin the last 10 years, that companies have been formed in the West Indian Islands for the purposes of Life Assurance, and those schemes being local, and consequently limited in their operations could not obtain insurers in sufficient numbers to form a proper estimate of the average duration of human life in these tropi cal regions; being also conducted at a comparatively greater expense, than the larger

institutions of Europe, their success bus not been very striking, whilst the rates of insurance were extravagantly high. The above company however has been started with the immense capital of hall a million sterling, and its operations ate to extend over the East and West Indies, ihe Canadas, Australia, the Cape of Good Hope, New Zealand, China, and in point of fact over the whole of that portion of the habitable globe, on which Europeans can exist, or the value of human life be calculated whether of natives or foreigners. So much has been written and urged on the subject of life assurance, that we have nothing to add, saving the following, which we clipped from a N. York paper.

Life Insurance. þÿ Worse than an InjiitEL. þÿ It is something more than wrong, it is criminal, for men with families dependent upon their labour for the means of existence to neglect the benefits of life insurance. We know of a man who died a few days in this city, leaving four young orphans without a dollar in the world, and not money enough to pay for his shroud. This man was a daily operator in stocks in Weils Street, and had formerly been in easy circumstances What a pity he had not been wise, and provident enough to have laid aside one shilling a day for life insurance, which would have secured to his children the sum of 5000 dollars at his death. He that provides not for his own family is worse than an infidel. þÿ New York Evening Minor.

THE POTATO DISEASE The following brief detail of experiments and their results with the diseased potatoes will oe found very interesting to our readers generally. The gentleman who made the experiments resides at Bris tol. " Having, as I believe, succeeded in tracing out the cause of the potato lat'use, the question naturally arose in my mind, what is the remedy? and 1 have ap,.iicd a scries of experiments to the solution of tiiat query. 1 will give the experiments and their results Experiment 1. 1 used soot in the following manner : þÿ 1 fiist took off many leaves which had become yellow, or in any way bitten by insects. 1 then applied the soot freely over the surface of the ground, and dusied the hacks ot the remaining leaves wilh it. This produced a decidedly beneficial effect þÿ the plants assumed a healthful appeaiance, and occasional application of the s uit has retained them iu a vigorous state. Experiment SI 1 used quick lime precisely in the same manner. The good effects were even more marked than with the soot þÿ the plants now look green and strong, and give no indications ol decay. The lime, however, should be applied þÿ at least lor a while þÿ every four or live days. Experiment 3 1 employed lime from the gas works This being extremely caustic, and emiiting a powerful effluvium, 1 merely put it between the ridges, taking care not to touch the plain. I observed that the aphides instantly hopped from the plants, and as long as the lime emitted its odour the plants kept free from insects, and looked healthy. Ex

perimenl 4. 1 washed the plants, and watered the ground with a solution of common salt, but little or no good resulted from the application. Experiment 5. i applied the salt dry and powdered, but it did no good, as the insect Continued devouring the plant while the salt remained upon the leaves. Experiment 6. I put some ignited sulphur in a row of pots at the edges of the ridges, in a direction for the wind to waft the vapour through the plants The effects were remarkable. The insects near the sulphur pots fell dead quickly, and those more distant became inactive. Experiment 7. 1 applied

1 1 1 Wood ashes reduced to powder, by dusiing the earth and leaves wiili tfietn This produced a good effect, hut requites to be none frequently Experiment 8 1 poured spints of turpentine between two ridges, and ihe vapour killed the insects, and 1 have seen none upon the leaves since. Experiment 9. 1 used camphor reduced to powder, but it did no good Experiment 10. 1 mixed sulpinuic acid and nitre, and tried the eflect of the gas generated by holding the pot containing the liquor under a plant at a lime. The aphides fell off immediately, and have not returned (a period 01 seven days) Experiment 11. 1 applied in the sumc way the vapour of muriatic acid, which also removed the insects, and the plants look healthy. Experiment 12. 1 used nitric acid in ihe same way, and with the same results. Expeiiment 13. 1 washed the leaves with a solution of Barbadoes aloes. The insects left the leaves, and have not returned (a period of three days). All the plants where ,tlie expeiimeuts appeared lo succeed now look strong and healthy, but as 1 do not think it safe to rely upon orc application, 1 am repeating them at intervals The application which appeared to be most efficacious was that with the spirits of luipetnine, but, taking into account the cost i>) t lie antidote, the facilities for applying it, and other collateral circumstances, i am induced <0 recommend for general adoption the occasional application of powdered quick lime The Oest time will be to apply it early in the morning, when ihe leaves of

DC/3 We nre indebted to a merchant of this city lor the following extract from a letter received from the City ot St. Domingo, and it will doubtless be perused with interest. ST. DOMINGO, JULY 10, 1847. We are now in (lie fourth year of Dominican independence, and the third session of its legislature has just drawn to a close. If any argument can possibly prove the incompatibility of a union between the Spanish and the franco African race, if evidence woie wanting to establish the marked and distinct nationul characteristics of the two people, the acis of this lust session of the Dominican Congress must set those questions at rest loi ever. The one sunk in apathy, degraded by every vice, and contending with mortal stiilc against the spirit of civilisation of the age, struggled in vain for 20 years to reduce the high minded Spaniards, whom adverse circumstances had placed in iis power to form pail and parcel of the exclusive race the Haytiens siill aspired to. The other bold speculative, and enterprising, enabled by a high sense ot honor ; n marked veneration lor religion and morality, is a suppliant at tiie throne of light, and seeks wub uidour to Iraieruixe itsell with the most illustrious nations of lire utiivetse. The Dominicans shook oil the Haytien yoke because it was a violent usurpation which strove to convert a happy and a virtuous community into slupid barbarians, an usurpation which deprived them of all natulal and political rights as men to seek their own pros pet ity and happiness; and the tern-

pei ate, decided and judicious manner in which they have conducted ibis revolution, maiked by no excesses, in which ihe authority of the laws never for a moment was suspended, eminently proves how tit they are to estimate the blessings of libei ty. Among the interesting acts of the late session, 1 may cite the municipal law, which has been amplified with many very important additions, and principles of government already required by these Dominican communities together with which the municipal revenues have been considerably augmented, in order to meet the extended range ol the prero gatives of these uselul institutions. Amendments have likewise been intioduced into the law lor the improved civil government of the provinces. Congress lias also passed an act for the incorporation of a company to open n macadamized road between Santiago and i'orto l'latn, which bv the surveys already made, w ill reduce lire present distance to nearly one third. The executive has been clothed witli the most ample powers for the promotion of immigration, funds have been placed at its disposal for the purpose "f assisting the indigent, and authority to grant concessions ol all public lands in parcels of 50 acres in full right and properly (ree of any charge w hatever to each immigrant, who is moreover exoneiatcd from all military service. That highly unpolitical vestige of Haytien legislation, that incubus upon the prosperity and advance item of any country, the imposition of patents or licenses lor pursuing any
kind ol iudustry, has been quite exploded.

i "i n i » Licenses arc now only reqili" d, for merchants, shopkeepers, distiller ies and billiard tables. All other trades and professions of whatsoever nature are free for natives as well as foreigners. The retail trade is also open to foreigners and all other vocations which require a license. The foreign consignee patent is rated at only eighty dollars. The custom house laws also have been completely remodelled, affording the utmost facilities and despatch to trade. The import and export of gold and silver with ail other metals and evety species of mineral productions ate declared free. Vessels arriving with immigrants, and all vessels touching at any of the ports without doing any trade, pay no port charges. Foreign vessels can freely load without restriction at any piace within the territory of the Dominican republic, and in certain cases can engage in the coasting trade. The chief articles which pay an export duty are wax, mahogany, dye woods, live stock, hides, and tobacco, which duty will also he shortly taken otf in toto The import duties now average 12 pr. cent. But the grandest and boldest measure of the session has been the reform of the currency, which has now become the law of the land. The Dominicans at the period when they shook oil the Haytien yoke, were without a shilling in their treasury, and were suffering at the time from a depreciated Haytien paper current at only one third its nominal value. They had then to support an active war, build and repair extensive fortifications, equip

and man a considerable naval fotce, supply the aiscnal witii war like stoies, and establish a constitutional Government. All this was accomplished without ditticulty, through the patriotism of the citizens. New issues of paper however were indispensable, which exceeding the sum requited lor the circulating medium of the country, caused a corresponding fluctuation and depreciaiion in its value, A» no country can possibly improve with a fluctuating monetary system, the Dominicaii Congress decided at once on taking up the paper now in circulation at its par v<i|uc in gold when issued, for which stock will tie given bearing five per cent inieicst redeemable in ten years; and further dcciecd the total reform and establishment of a new circulating medium in sterling silver, and paper redeemable in silver on demand, at par with all other civilised nations; for the currying of which into execution there is a considerable sum now in the treasury vaults, and any deficiency can be readily supplied by disposing of a part of the national piopetty, for which due provision has been made. Thus has this young republic braved all its adverse ciicumslances without incurring a shilling of debt, and now it tenders to the world a land flowing with milk and honey, possessed of a soil unsurpassed by any in the universe, blessed with a climate that can vie with the tnosl delicious regions, with liberty of conscience, freedom of indusirv, and with unenlightened Government to protect aid respect the lights of all its inhabitants.
The rich mines which this island contains, after having been closed for more than three centuries, are now revealed and opened to lite entcrpiiso of the world.

W«a.i ' ' - The capitalist, the agriculturalist, the artisan, will all find in this new country the most abundant resources for the advantageous employment of their active energy and talents. Add to all this the exiremely favorable position which this long neglected country occupies in the very centre ol commercial enterprixe and movement ; its proximity to Europe, being as it were one of the outposts of the new world stretching towards the old one, which bids fair to cause it soon to rank with the richest states of America.

You will gather a fair notion of thp daring and audacity of the guerillas from their repeated atrocities under the walls of the city. Within the past thirty six hours another man has been hanged by them, almost within gun shot of our batteries. The victim was one of the most active police officers, a Pane, named Miller He and a Frenchman were out riding when they were " lassoed" and carried into the woods. 1 he I' renchman was released, but Miller is said to have been put to death as slated. Parties were out most of the day and night of yesterday, in search of the perpetrators of the outrage, and seven Mexicans were seized on the roads and brought in. þÿ Five of these proved to be gentlemen bound to Medelin; hut the others are suspicious characters, and the Governor has imprisoned them to await further examination. One ol them was taken on the horse which Miller was riding when attacked. We are yet withou' authentic, intelligence from Mexico of a later date than the 12th inst., and nothing of especial interest up to that time There seems U) he no doubt of Santa tuna's intention to make a stand against General Scott at some point between Puehla and the capital, arid our next arrival from our little army may tell us of another Cerro Gordo allair. From the Cape Veri> Islands. þÿ The linxbury Gazelle publishes the following extract ol a letter from an officer of the Navy dated Fort Frays, May 27 : þÿ 'l'he revolution in Portugal has not heen without its effect in these islands. An insurrection is hourly expected at (his place, but as the par tizans of I Ion Miguel number ten to one of those in favor of Donna Maria, it will probably take place with little or no bloodshed, unless it should break out in the night, when throat cutting aud plunder will be the order of perfoi mances for the occasion. The officers of (lie. garrison are nearly all for Don Miguel, and have been sent out here for political offences against Donna Maria; this fact will probably tend to keep down any serious disturbances; hut there are great numbers of convicts on the island, who, of course, are on hand for a riot of any description þÿ The Governor General received his appointment from Donna Marin's government and will be obliged to " cut his slick," as the Yankees elegantly express it. We are to sail on our leeward cruise to the coast in a few dais, and will go as far south us Benguela. 1 suppose there will he a similar revolution in the Portuguese province of Angola, as soon as they leain of the change at home.

Taylor. þÿ A paragraph is going the rounds, In the effect that Major General Taylor lias announced his determination to resign his ollice, on the first day of September next. Such is not the case. General Taylor has made no such announcement ; hut he intends to appl y, on the first of September next, for a short leave of absence from duty, in order to attend to his private ulluiis, which needs his cure. It seems that an extensive plantation on tfic Mississippi, which the General owns, was recently ovei flown, by which it received much damage, and it is to repair that us well as to attend to some other private matters, and see his family and friends, that he will seek a temporary reiiternent from service. He purposes leaving his post on or about the first of November next, and returning immediately after he accomplishes what he de signs. We repeat that General Taylor has not aunouueed his intention to resign.

It is estimated that there are 587 languages and genera! dialects in Europe. 937 in Asia, 220 in Afiica, aud 1201 in America in nil nearly 3000. We ate obliged to refer the transition of languages either to an indefinite antiquity of nations, or to distiuct races of men. 1 he principle is the same in all þÿ names of things and names of actions with qualities ol things, modes of action, and relations of place. Fowers of voice are as natural to man as to animals and birds, and border tribes weie likely to interchange theii sounds. Monosyllables were the primitive sounds, and syllable compounds would be results. Hence, nil the fundamental tongues are monosyllabic as to generic ideas, and coinpounds species and varieties. 1 he Sanscrit, Chinese, Welsh, Greek, Hebrew, German

Ate , are formed on this principle. Man appears to have vocal organs of great flexibility, and these, iu every lamily, cave, or union of caves, would he the bases of a dialect. Two or more families would, of course, by association, club their stock of words, and fortuitous circumstances would expand the dominion of some one, and generate in time a nearly common language within physical boundaries. Vocal sounds are the natural utterance of the human voice, similar in man to the sounds uttered by birds and animals, and by which they express a few general ideas, without the complication aud composition efleclcd by human reason and gi eater compass of utterance. Frimitivc sounds, or monosyllables, are, thcrefoic, a kin to each other in all the elder languages, as in Sanscrit. Chinese, Welsh, Ate.; and all their words are composite, t. c consist of the genus united to another, or to two or three to discriminate the species of the idea. Other languages are dialects compounded out of these, as English, French, Spanish, Italian. &r.. and further complicated by words derived from one another. The Chinese have 214 radical words and signs of them, the Welsh about as many ; and out of these by synthesis othr words are formed, to the number of fifty or sixth thousand. Differences arise from the structure of the vocal organs, or from imitation of parents, or at present from corruptions. or as written from different poweig of letters. There are 20,001) words in Spanish ; 25.( 00 in Latin ; from 22 to 25.000 in English ;
30 000 in French; 45 000 in Italian; 50,000 in Greek ; and 80 000 in Gorman. There are 1700 radical words in llcbiew, and 300 Chahiaic woids in Ihu Bible.

The firs) languages would consist of open vowel sounds, and their stops or consonants to discriminate the sense of the vowel sounds Once formed, the Pedagogue would introduce rules, and give to a language its scholastic forms. Accident would give the fust links. The use of one part of the glottis, the preference of teeth, lips, nose, tongue, &c., would afford the key, and the rest would be radiation from that key. Usage would make one form of utterance as easy as another, and, hence, the strange diversity in which every animal sound is adopted and systematized. The first voice is noise similar in principle 1o the drone of bagpipes, and the words and language are inflections and modulations. Even the vo-vel sounds vary with the parts employed in producing first sounds. It is an epoch when comtemplativc man first began to represent ideas and sounds by drawings, and a greater epoch when these hieroglyphics wete abbreviated into current written characters. These discoveries were, however, simultaneous, since different people made different abbreviations.

An Eccentric Clergyman. þÿ The Cm cinnati Advertiser tells a story of. an eecen trie clergyman who, not being a very animated and interesting preacher, was often deseited by his flock, at least by parts of them, on the Sabbath. The old gentleman finally adopted rather a novel method of keeping the delinquents up to the point of duty. When any family was absent two or three Sabbaths in succession, Mr S. would publicly state to the congregation, that, as JMr. þÿ þÿ \s family had been for some lime absent from public worship, he presumed there was sickness or trouble in their household, and would appoint a prayer meeting at their house on the next Tuesday afternoon. The off gentleman, on one occasion, caught ttie wanderers by the following piece of "guile." On one Sabbath afternoon lie told his people that he should take a short journey t tie next day. and be absent lor a short time, but he would take care that some person should come from Boston and supply his desk the next Sabbath. On the next Sabbath morning the meeting house was filled. The whole town turned out to see the Boston minister. Thev wailed awhile in eager expectation of entrance, when in marched the Kev. Mr. S. , and walked by the broad aisle, as he had been accustomed to do many years gone by. On ascending tiis pulpit he smiled graciously upon his large audience, and said " 1 am glad my dear brethren that 1 fiave you out. You are all here, as you ought to lie, and I hope your minds are pre pared to receive instruction. 1 came from

Boston yesterday myself" I\1eni>els.soiin þÿ 1 yesterday" (says a Now York publication,) visited Mendelssohn, the celebrated composer. lioyal Economy þÿ The King of the French takes particular care of his clothes ; and I onee saw him in a very -bad humour because lie had torn his coal against a door. THE WMl , 4-e SaNTA þÿanna s RUMOURED DICTATORSHIP. I'Tom the New Orleans Delta, July 4. In our paper of Friday, we staled genetally that, up to the 12th ult, (our latest data from the city of Mexico.) Santa Anna had not been proclaimed, nor Lad lie proclaimed himself, Dictator. We now give at len.oh the article on that subject, from El Monitor Ilepublicano, of the 12th ult. That paper says : þÿ Many times have we taken our pen to contradict the rumors about the revolutionary establishment of a military dictatorship, and as many times have we abandoned i , the whole appearing to us unworthy ol credit, and without the semblance of a foundation, It appeared to us, and it yet appears, that only the infuriated enemies of Santa Anna and of the country could, for effect, have seized upon this disgraceful and intamous rumor ; yet it has been propagated in such a manner, and so extended, ihat we hasten to give it the lie as an evidence ol our good faith, and from a conviction of the tremendous evils such a rumor may bring upon our devoted country. þÿ When Santa Anna tendered his resignation, he was undoubtedly calumn ated, it being assumed that he covertly designed to establish this fatal alternative: Either Congress will not accept my resignation, but d.-lay action by a recess, nnd 1 remain thus in absolute power þÿ or, it will accept it, and then the army is the power to place in my hands the dictatorship. This calumny has been made to disappear, since the question of a recess was agitated in the Chambers, and

the partisans who wished to use it for purposes of scandal, have shown themselves to a certain extent, satisfied with the recess þÿ some fearful of exhibiting the spectacle, day after day, of the shameful desertion <4 deputies þÿ others, desirous of removing every obstacle to power. Of 1 lie fit si, it is said there was a sentiment of honor and of attachment to the representative system ; of the latter, that such vile adulation, such cringing subserviency, to the depository of a power adequate to all circumstances, was bitterly censured. But this combination frustrated, the rumor of a dictatorship has been renewed ; and for ourselves, we are satisfied it can only come from the secret enemies of the war. Certain it is, that, in circumstances like ours, the people most devoted to their liberties, have sacrificed them to the common safety ; certain it is that they have granted omnipotent power for the purpose ot avoiding, at the time, internal discord, and of repelling foreign invasion ; but the circumstances in which we are placed would, on every hand, render this merely despotic and futile attempt inefficacious and fatal. Do they believe that Santa Anna is ignorant of the fact that, in uil the States, with few exceptions, a fatal contest is going on between the governors and the legislatures, the germ of bitterness and liigl tful dissolution ? Do they believe that Santa Anna is ignoiant of the fact that the per, pie would not suffer this dictatorship, even under tlie auspices of brilliant victories ? Do they
believe that he does not know what ihc mission of the ar my is in these circumstances, reduced to the alternative id conqueting or dying fur the independence of the country ?

Sincere Republicans, we say it with grief), perhaps Federalists, by change faitlifui have, by their numberless errors, fastened nn indelible stain upon our institutions. From them have the enemies of our popular system derived their shameful arguments þÿ a system denationalized and perverted by those who should have been its delenders. Errors, however, and passions hv no means affect principles; the federation is held responsible and yet the federation has, indeed, neither been tried nor understood. The federation, which is, indeed, a confraternity of the people for strengthening (Itemselves by recognizing a centre of action, has been converted into a cry of dissolution, which has made us yet weaker, exhibiting to the world the spectacle of that hostile inactivity by which Mexico, incombating a foreign tbuetny, has been embarrassingly beset. For the chimerical attempt at a dictatorship, such as the enemies of Santa Anna and of the country suppose it, the common consent, or, lather, the sanction and proclamation of the Slates, were indispensable ; there was need of the blindest confidence and of the most intimate relations between the depository of power and the people; antecedent acts of the most honorable kind were necessary, as well ns mutual confidence between the people and the army, whose ambition has created interests distinct from the interests of the masses. At least was it important to foresee that this Sacrifice of a suspension of our institutions Would restore them to us sound and vigorous

tendering so tremendous a power prolific of good. þÿ In other times, from misfortune, the Executive has held this omnipntenrv for the public good. And what was gained T Food for aristocratic pride, some miserable contracts, support to favoritism, pretexts for ridiculous and ruinous persecutions! þÿ the hook of Open history, and Rome, the republics Italy, ol and all the people of the European continent, furnish lessons to the vile sycophants who now flatter with a dictatorship the ears of the thoughtless. þÿ On the other hand, what contempt, what execration would not lie deserve who should, with arms, produce a revolution, to destroy the existing government, betraying us, to our invaders ? There are not words to describe all tile odium, all the punishment, to which such infamy would he entitled. And what should we say if the army or the government were to be converted into factions, usurping powers not legitimately devolved upon them? What name would such a revolution in our circumstances merit. þÿ Different is the course, according to our notion, which the government and the people ought to pursue. The first, consistent with its >ath. ought to seek its strength in morality, respect the social guarantees and the public liberties, use the immense power it now possesses for something really great, and the result vvill be a conciliation of the public confidence. The Stales, on their part, ought to assist t lie government The question of independence is not that of the district, hut of

the eoiire republic. Thev ought to contri bate to the common safety with ail their res 'UrCes, with all their strength, even with heii blood i liev ought to concur in the general plan operation, and confide in the of government, and not saciifice a positive good tot a inert! chimera. This wo believe to be the true m xlt- ol safety."

The consequences, no doubt, were more seriou titan they would be now. Vesalius hardly escaped the claws of the Inquisition, and died during his expiatory pilgrimage to the Holy Land. In England, indeed, our decent respect for the dead, which lead us to posipotie interment as long as possible, is a tolerable security against biting tuiiied alive. Ether and its Effects þÿ l)r. James H. Pickford has addressed to the Morning Chronicle a solemn warning against the use of ether, lie denies that the insensibility which it produces is no worse titan that of drunkenness oi asphyxia. There is a chemical alteration in the vital constituents of the blood ; for not only is that deprived of its oxygen, and of the power of coagulation like the black vitiated blood of malignant and putrid fevers þÿ hut the corpuscules whence fibrin is formed are actually dissolved. þÿ Hence the blood takes a long lime to regain its life supporting, flesh forming character; wounds show everted edges and refuse to heal; and the patient often sinks into death. The use of ether also tends to produce tubercular consumption of the lungs; in thirty cases of death alter the use of ether, in the Dublin Hospitals, the deaths could be t taccd to recent tubercles, believed to he the product of the ether.

Trial of M. Teste and his Confederates. Those very extraordinary judicial proceedings, about which so much interest is felt In France commenced on the 8th inst., before the Court of Peers The parties accused are General Cuhit'res, and Al. Al. Teste, Purmentier, and Pcllapra, Peers of Prance, for escroquerie (sw indling), bribery, and corruption. The following is the subject oi the charges : þÿ In 182t> a company was formed by Parmentier and several others for working a coal field at tiouhenans ; and soon after the commencement of operations a mine ol it was discovered within the allotment of ground of the coal company, lor the working ol which a distinct license was required fiom the Government ; and General Cubit-res and his partner, Al. I'armentier, entered into negotiations with the Minister, Al. Teste, for tiie purchase of this privilege. These negotiations were carried on at different intervals for several years ; and on the 14th January, 1842, General Cubieres wrote a l< Iter to his partner, Al. I'armentier, in which lie stated ' that the Government was in the hands of greedy and corrupt men," and represented himself as able to secure the support necessary to the success of their enterprise through the medium of this mercenary cabinet. A long intrigue followed, in which shares arid money exchanged hands in a most unaccountable manner. M. Teste had apportioned to him 25 scrip shares in the Goohenans Company, hut it is not shown that he ever received or held any shares or benefit in the corcern ; but that, on the contrary, upon a

re-nrrangement of the company's affairs, these shares remained in the hands of General Cubit-res, and were eventually destroyed. It was the general impiession thai Cubieres was the chiel conspirator in these proceed ings, wh -n I'ellapra ab-conded, and a secret correspondence was brought to light, lending to shew that Cubieres had been the dupe,

rather than the original concocier ol the fraud. His examination is, however, so lull of contradictions, that it is scarcely possible to believe a word he says The proceedings are carried on before the Chamber of l'eers in such an irregular, desultory manner, that it is scarcely possible to unravel all the entangled meshes of the plot. The trial had lasted sevetal da\s, when the wife of Al. 1'allapia sent in to the Chancellor u number of documents, which almost legally proved that Al. i'ellapra Imd paid to Al. Teste the sum of ninety three thousand francs. This was corroborated by his banker's account, and evidem e to the same effect by M 1'ellapra's ugens de change and his attorney. The hitler almost conclusively proved that the money was paid to Al. Teste, and General Cubieres declared that though he did not choose to be the informer, he had before heard the notary say to Al. l'ellapra that the money had been paid over to Al. Teste. An investment of about 90 000 francs in ions lioyoux was also clearly proved to have been made by the younger Teste about the same date. In spite of this conclusive evidence, Al Teste, on Monday, cross examined the witnesses with all the dispassionate adroitness of a counsel acting as a feed advocate for a third party. At the rising of the court at six o'clock, M. Teste against whom such a mass of unexpected evidence has been brought, appeared, until the last proofs were given, to be the least affected individual in the crowded hall ; but when the actual proof

of investment of money at the treasury was adduced, his coinage gave way ; his criminality, in his own opinion, became so completely established, that he literally withered, and from being an erect powerful manshtunk iu a moment in the view of the spectator into a miserable cowering altitude. Upon retiring to the apartments of the Luxembourg, Al. Teste made two attempts at suicide, which however failed. The chancellor an i the grand ieferendary were sent for, and it is said that Al. Teste admitted his guilt to tliein. At the sitting of Tuesday, a letter from Al. Teste was read by the Registrar He threw himself on the mercy of the court, declaring that, after what had come out in the evidence the preceding day, he considered the evidence definitely closed as far as he was concerned, and that he accepted beforehand, whatever decision the court might con e to relative to him in his absence. He thought such a couise more fitting than to persevere in an unavailing resisiance. The counsel from the eo accused addressed the court, all admitting the guilt of their clients, but praying lor mercy, Al. LKIiault made a strong appeal to the court in favour, not of M. Teste, but of his son, who, lie said, was wholly ignorant of the transaction, and an innocent actor therein ; he concluded his appeal in the words of iiossuet, " Alerey is an iutegial part of justice." After hearing the counsel for all the prisoners, the Court deliberated, and acquitted Geneial Cubieres of swindling, but found him and all the other prisoieia
guilty of bribery and corruption, and the sentence will probably be delivered in Paris this day.

OitiGiN of England's National Debt. þÿ The existing debt had a most fitting commencement, viz., an agreement to repay a a debt of Charles 11. At tlmt time there was a kind of paper money issued bv goldsmiths as a ' receipt for coin,' lodged with ihem on deposit. Charles, always in a strait for money, and surrounded by prostitutes and a most profligate set of men, was unable to borrow; his credit was gone. He, therefore, with his worthy coadjutors contrived to cieate a panic, during which he induced goldsmiths and merchants to lodge their money, £(104.203, in the exchequer for security. As soon as this was done, he abstracted the money and spent it in his revels. This sum, hearing six per cent interest, commenced that English debt which is now £800,000,000 þÿ The people of England have paid interest on the money Charles stole, and gave to his women, £40 000 per annum, lor 181 years, making £1,240,000 or $32,000,000, and the debt is mi nearer extinguishing than betorc. Gradually increasing during the eighteenth century, the debt rose to £203,403,013, in 103 In the following 22 years, which is the estimate for the life of a generation, it was increased £340,000,000! Suppose every generation should hot row a like sum, who would pay? Surely .Mr. I'itt and his generation had no exclusive light to borrow. Of thi i ty generations which passed awav from the Norman conquest down to the French war, each one had as much right lo borrow us that of Mr. Bin, and nearly every one had

as much necessity. Suppose they had done so, where would have been Ins ability to borrow ? The generations that have pnssed away since the contraction of the debt have quietly submitted to pay its interest, hut the one now in being has begun strongly to question both his right to borrow at all the justice of the debts lie did not contract, and the equity of continuing to pay. When this matter comes once to he seriously discussed, the death knell of the funding system may be considered as being struck. þÿ Democratic lie view.

The Influence of Woman þÿ Deprived of an equal voice in the government and councils of nations, and of the chances to reveal heroism and physical power on the battle field, woman has exercised hut a partial influence over the (ate of mankind. If savage, barbarous and semi civilized epochs she has been scarcely more than a creature to bring forth the progeny and bear the burthens of the world. 1 Lodging and bowed down in the wigwam of the savage þÿ following the trails of armies to kindle camp fees and prepare ihe fond ot the warrior þÿ tilling the fields of her little more civilized husband taskmaster, or miuisleiing (nun slave marts to the passions of pandering man, as all Asia reveals her þÿ what has woman been hut a trampled flower, stiil leautifrd in its rniuplucked and cast by the moment its odor had produced satiety. I low unlike that glorious being who in the Garden ot E Jen was given to man to solace and beguile him þÿ I" fill 'he spaces of solitude with lire beatitude of heaven Her weakness, innocence and con fiding nature were then, what ihcv should ever have remained, the elements ol iranscen-

dei t strength. In that fair and tremulous beauty, which was as heaven itself, lived ihe angels who forsook the earth when woman descended from her primitive being. Step by step, was the fall accelerated, until in ages but just gone, nothing but tears weie left to assert the humanity of her race- Woman is only inferior to man in great physical power þÿ in all the fine and heroic sentiments, she is his equal if no' his sn erior, and generations, in whatever age ot darkness or light, take their hue and shape from the impress of her power. If she he trampled and debased, so will be her children þÿ if she be pure and beautiful in heart and life, her progeny will he the same. In whatever condition, her original nature has never been fully obscured. Gleams of the heroic and heavenly have shot out from the darkness þÿ Spartan and Roman mothers have answered for the sex þÿ and even the wilderness has not wanted lofty specimens of the true woman among the savages of our race. Give woman the place of Companionship which God gave her, let her be the counsellor and friend of man, and the scale of our civilization will never droop on the side ol humanity.

A Farmer's Barometer. þÿ A writer in the Georgia Farmer gives directions for making cheap a barometer, to aid in foretelling the weather. He takes a stick three feet long, and attaches to the butt end a phial, full of air, of couise, and corked tight. The stick is then suspended in a horizontal position on a pivot wheie it will leadily turn, say a thread tied near its centre. þÿ When the storin is coming on, the air outside is lighter than that within the phial : of course the phial sinks, and indicates a change in the atmosphere. Such a barometer may be made in ten minutes, and some ol our philosophical farmers will incline to have barometers of their own manufacture þÿ American Taper.

He received me with Chinese politeness, and asked me to sit down, and offered me tea and his pipe þÿ two things always at hand in a Chinese house, and perleetly indispensable. Having civilly declined Ins offer, 1 asked permission to examine his hatching house þÿ to which place he immediately led the way. 1 he Chinese cottages, generally, are wretched buildings of mud and stone, with damp earthem floors, scarcely fit for cattle to sleep on,

and remind one of what Scottish cottages were a few years ago, but which now, happily are among the things that wore. My new friend's cottage was no exception to the general rule. The Relations of England mid Spain þÿ The Island of Cuba. The recent debu'e in the British Parliament on the Spanish bond question, in which our amiable but excitable friend, Lord Pal merston, went out of the way to " warn" the non-paying States of the world, may be of great importance to the United Stales, as will be seen hereafter, it originated in a motion of Lord George Bentinck, that a petilion be presented to her Majesty, praying that she would take such steps as might be deemed advisable, to secure payment to British subjects of moneys loaned the Spanish government, amounting to the no small sum of forty-six millions of pounds sterling, or about $230 000000. In the course of the debate, Lord Bentinck, who is a sort of Santa Anna in England, in more ways than one, called upon the government, to insist on making Spain pay what she owed, and laid it down as according to the law of nations, thai one government is entitled to demand of another redtess for wrongs done against the subjects of the com plaining State, and if it be denied, that it may be euforced in way of reprisal, oi in any other way of which the complaining power may be capable. So much for the principle laid down in the debate. Now let us take a glance across the Atlantic. The largest and most valuable island of the West Indies is Cuba þÿ the length of winch is seven hundred and sixty miles, and the breadth ninety. The soil is extremely fertile ; it abounds with mines and produces excellent sugar, coffee, honey, wax. tobacco,

&.c. And what is of more importance, it is actually tbe key to the Gull of Mexico. þÿ This fair island is owned by Spain, who dirives a great revenue from it, and Spain is indebted to England to the amount of S230.000.000. On the same side of the Atlantic, there is an immense republic known as the United Slates ; a nation which, in the short space of seventy years, lias grown to he one of the most powerful countries in the world lis present grandeur is brilliant beyond all example, and it is daily extending its territory, it is at present at war with a neighboring republic, the result of which will be, (hat it will get another accession of territory front its hostile neighbor. This en / assunt. It happens that the contest for the commerce and wealth of the world is between this great republic ol the West and its gieat rival, England, and it happens, moreover, that certain indications point towards Cuba one day, not vuiv distant, becoming, not perhaps, a part and parcel of the Western republic, hut under her guardianship, by which it would become much more powerful than it is, and by which it would obtain exclusive control

I 1 I II I - ''-''I i a II I « over the American seas, Now, England cannot but sec this; and seeing it, she would like to prevent it; and us she never was at a loss for finding expedients, she is not in this case, and has in our opinion already found one very applicablel o the case, wuu b is the assertion of the piiueiplc luid down by Lord Bentinck, and coincided in by our amiable peace loving friend Lord Palmerston, in the recent debate on the Spanish bonds Spain cannot pay the forty six millions of pounds she owes British subjects. Lord Palmeiston gives " warning" that he will force her to pay it by reprisal, if necessary ; or. in other words, by scizute of territory. What part of her territory would he seize? Certainly the most valuable part, and that is tbe island of Cuba þÿ a distant colony from tbe mother country. By sti/.tng it England would accomplish two purposes, viz: payment of the money due her subjects, and pet haps obtain a cheek on her rival, the great American republic þÿ and the command over a part of the American seas, ll she is determined to apply the principle in one case, she probably is in another, and lite next country to which she will apply it is Mexico þÿ then the South American Slates þÿ in each gaining territory and aggtandizemt lit. The matter then resolves itself into this þÿ that England is desirous of securing territory on the American continent for tbe purpose of checking the growth of the United States; that she has her eye on Cuba at the present hour, and that we may soon expect to hear

of her attempting a la, " the man with the white hat," to put the principle she asset te<J in force, and getting possession of the island of Cuba if possible. Now, we have a principle, which we asserted as far back as the presidency of Mr. Monroe þÿ which is peculiarly applicable to the case ill hand, and that is, that no European intervention with the American continent will bo tolerated by the United States, II we maintain (h it, and England maintain hers, the two countries must, of necessity, come in conflict. Well, what then ? þÿ Ibid.

ETHER Its Value in benmjitting Patients unsensible To Pain during Surgical Operations. þÿ Who shall decide when doctors disagree ? Most certainly not us brethren of the grey goose -quill þÿ and yet we may l>e permitted to canvass both sides ttf all questions þÿ perhaps give an opinion, or an expla ration, which may go fat to prove that both B re rn the right, and yet both in the wrong, as were the knights in the olden time with toeir shield of immortal tame. Those w ho have performed successful operations alter subjecting patients to its influence laud it to Ihe skies, and eulogize it as a heaven-born discovery. On the other hand, it is urged that the insensibility which it produces is widely different from that of intoxication or asphyxia þÿ that it occasions a chemical alteration in tire vital constituents of the blood, and produces tubercules in the lungs which cause death after the patient has to all appearances recovered. We recur to this subject, because we have been informed that Or. D. Pretto hns lately pei formed two minor operations successfully, having caustd the patients to inhale the Ether þÿ that no pain was felt by ttiem, arid that both are now recovered, and in excel lent health. This we were extremely glad to hear, for the discovery is doubtless a valuable one, but it should be remembered þÿ " What is one man's meat is another man's poison," That whilst the exhibition of Eiher may be perfectly harmless, as to its ultimate effects on some constitutions it may be cer- þÿ

tain death to others, such as those of high nervous organizations, or those who may be predisposed to consumption, and who carty Within them the seeds of the complaint, which such a stimulant as the inhalation of so powerful an agent as Etherial vapour may cause to fructify. .Most persons have seen how w idely different were the effects produced by inhaling the laughing gas. which was a few years since a popular chemical experiment ; nod therefore it is almost certain þÿ reasoning from analogy that the use of Ether will produce equally strange and startling contradictions. It is a new and therefore fashionable agent, and may prove a useful assistant to the scientific operator, but the subject demands a rigid investigation to determine the nature of its action on t he system, before it siiouid be indiscriminately used.

Elegance ofr Form. þÿ The most common cause of a high shoulder is th be found in the practice of undressing girls' necks as low as the hanging of their clothes will permit. þÿ Instead of their shoulder straps of their dress being, as they should he, fairly supported across the shoulder, they often þÿ indeed most Commonly þÿ either only rest on the rounded Upper part of the deltoid muscles or are actually far down on the aims; in consequence of which the dress, having little or no suspension on the shoulders, is constancy dropping, and the girl is Continually hitching up the shoulder, fiom which the shoulder Strap Vhrts't easily slips, and thus the elevating mtiSeles, becoming stronger on that side, pull the shoulder permanently up, and produces VCrV ugly appearance. 13ut the mischief does not stop here, for, though there is really tio disease of the spine vet this constant hitching up of the shoulder causes the head and the neck to be thrown to the other side, whilst the chest is thrown out to the same side, and thus a lateral curvature of the spine is produced, and a girl's figure is spoiled for the simple purpose of uncovering her neck as fas as possible, which, as well for decency as for the preservation of the child's health, ought to be covered. Many parents have been thus the real cause of their daughter's distortion, if not of more serious consequences ; and therefore, in growing giils, who have the least disposition to slip their shoulders out of their dress, most especial care

should be taken to prevent the possibility of keeping up this habit by having the dress made so high that it cannot slip down ; and then the sensation of its slipping being lost, the child no longer continues to hitch up her shoulder, and, by a little attention to her proper carriage, the mischief, if not of long standing, may be got rid of..

For five or six wedis two sheepish looking persons are seen dangitng about on each other's arms, looking at waterfalls, or making mottling calls, or guzzling wine and cake; then everything falls into a monotonous routine ; the wife sits on one side of the hearth, the husband at the other and little quarrels, little pleasures, little cares and little children, gradually gather round them This is What ninety nine out of one hundred find to be the delights of love and matrimony."

RUSSIA. The au'horilies at St Betersburgh have just received a report of the operations in the Caucasus, which opens with an account of the failure of the storming of the fortified village ofGengebil, in Daghestan, on the part of the Russians. Count Woronzow himself led the attack, which consisted of ten hat talions of infantry, several divisions ot dragoons, Cossacks, and militia. 1 hr commanding generals under him were Count Augutinske Dolgorwiki, Count Belutow Kotesbue, &c. The attack was made after lengthened preparations, and after several breaches had been made on the previous day On the morning of the Kith June two columns, one under the command of Colonel Oherlinm, penetrated simultaneously into the village, but at length, though supported by the re serve, were driven back by the Murides, and were compelled to retreat into the camp, whither the second column, commanded by Colonel Jendokinow, was also compelled to retire without having been able to penetrate even as far as the first column. The encounter is described as sanguinary in the extreme. The mountaineers permitted the Russian troops to come close to the walls before they opened their fire, and when ilia latter had forced their way into the interior of the village, thev found unlooked for obstacles; for example logemeui.s concealed in the earth, from which a deadly fire was discharged, fortified caverns, dwellings which were covered with sham roofs, and which gave way beneath the besiegers, who clambered upon

them and fell upon the swords of the Muri des. The obstinate defence of (be mountaineers convinced Count Woronzow that the place can only be taken by the irresistible force of artillery, and he has therefore, for the present, given up any further attack upon Gengebil. There fell in the fight of the 15th of June, two majors, six superior ollieers, and 119 privates: wounded, twenty-eight staff and superior officers, and 453 privates. The Augshui gh (Sozelte states that on the 8th June a terrible combat took place between a Russian division, commanded by General Lepiski, and the mountaineers, under the orders of Mohammed Jubu. Nearly 5000 fell on the field, neither party claiming the victory. The Circassians are greatly in want of gunpowder, paying, it is said 300 Turkish piastres the pound for it.

þÿPITCAIRN SISLAND. Her Majesty's brig Spy arrived off this island on the 2(!th of February, about 10 o'clock in tbe morning, and was hoarded by George Adams and some more natives shortly after she hove to. George Adams is the son of the celebrated John Adams, the father of the colony. Went ashoie in cutter, piloted by George Adams. Landplace a very small sandy beach with many rocks, and in the least breeze impracticable. We were met on the beach by some of the natives, who cordially welcomed us to Bitþÿcairn I s sland, and showed us the way to the market place up a steep and rugged 'path, winding along the cliff, and through a beautiful variety of all kinds of tropical flowers and shrubs. The scene when we arrived at the þÿ summit was picturesque in the extreme. þÿ The whole of the natives, men, women, and children, headed by Mr. Nopps, t lie schoolmaster, had assembled in a space of about half an acre square, carpeted with thick soft grass, and canopied overhead by the spreading branches of the cocoa nut tires roasted calves, lambs, þÿ&c , to meet the strangers, ail of them dressed in their gayest. Their welcome was waim, all of them advancing and shaking us by tie hand and addressing ns in perfectly good English. V\ e were extremely pleased by their quiet and decorous behaviour. As soon as we had made acquain lance with

hem all, we were ic.l through gently winding paths to the principal village, where the tSotirt house and church stands, as there were one or two slight disagreements, about land, Which they wished to be brought before Lieut. Wooldridge, commander of the Spy, end who very speedily disposed of them without their having evinced, either during the investigation or afterwards, the least feeling of discontent or displeasure- The Church is a neat building, well arranged, with ft pulpit and benches, and is used as. Well for a courthouse as a church. Mr. NoppS, the schoolmaster, performs the various offices. We were shown the old gun belonging to the Bounty that had been under Water for fifty six years, and which was now lying near the court-house. We visited old þÿAdam house s and grave, the last of which is situated in a beautiful spot next to his þÿwile s with eatables, which was obliged to lie of! grave, and kept in trim order. After rambling about, and visiting one or two of the inhabitants who were not well (one of whom had wounded himself with his gun while out shooting goats a short time before we arrived, hut was doing well), we returned to dinner, which had been prepared for us at M'< þÿjoy house, s and consisted of pork, yarn, and sweet potatoes. Each family on the island take it in turn to entertain strangers when they arrive, and never accept ary leward. Their food is principally vegetables. of which they have almost every kind, and twiee a- week either meat or fish, but

ihete is difficulty in getting the latter, as the fishing ground is bad and water very deep. The animals on the island are goats, which are wild, pigs, and fowls. Their houses are the perfection of cleanliness and good order, and each person has his plot of ground to cultivate. Their form of government is simple. They elect a magistrate every twelve months, upon which occasion every man and woman above eighteen is entitled to a vote, and, if married before that age, they are allowed a vote in consequence þÿ The magistrate then chooses an assistant, and ihe remainder of the people choose again another, who acts as a sort of check which is, indeed, little wanted þÿ for there is no place in the world where such perfect unanimity and good feeling exist as in this island. The number of inhabitants is one hundred and thii þÿty four, but ihe island can support many more, and they increase but slowly þÿ The island itself is only four miles and a half in circumference. We heard with pleasure, that though several whalers touch there, yet, in no instance, had any impropriety been committed. Forty-six whalers, mostly Americans, had called during the year !S4fi. They all appeared to talk of Adams with the greatest respect, and seemed to have s strong fueling of the crime that their ancestors committed in mutinying. They talked in the must affectionate loyal w v of "our þÿQueen, and appeared exceedingly proud of being English, but complained that they were so neglected, the " þÿSpy having Irecn t fret first

man-of-war which had visited them for more than three veeis. Tliev, however, were quite satisfied when told that this exigencies of the service had iatelv -prevented their being visited so often. They begged earnestly fur a visit by a man-of-war ns often as she could ire spared from other duties; but as George Adams remarked, they could not complain, as the Government had already been kinder 'to them than they deserved. Before our leaving, the

The letters of Tue-Fooug »he Mandarin. It is with groat satisfaction that I find it in my power to lay heioie the public another letter from my sagacious friend Tae-boong. The learned philosopher has spent the lew days he has been among us to great advantage, and has probably in that time acquit ed

quite as correct views of our national peculiarities as do most <d those clear-sighted and discriminating natives ul a net lain litilo island, who, after stairing at the ladies in Broadway and dining once or twice at the Aslor. hurry home to write a honk ouAmcrica. Such however, is far lroin being the

intention of the venerable Tae- Foong. lie does not pretend to uuders and by ruiuition things of which he belore hud no conception, and his heart is too noble and manly to cherish for un instant the intention ot abusing those from whom he bus experiencoo nothing but kindness. In truth my learned friend has been treated, since his arrival, with that distinction w hich is due to the august Monarch whom he represents, and to his own high character as a philosopher. He has been courier! and admired by all classes; smiled upon by the ladies, feasted bv the Corporation, and it is even rumored that the faculty of Columbia College at one time seriously contemplated bestowing upon him the honorary Uegiee ol doctor of laws, and appointing him to deliver a Chinese salutatory before that venerable institution, but to the grievous disappointment of the public, their resolution to this etiect was voted down, il being suggested that his odd appearance miglu cause unseemingly uttering among the young ladies at " Commencement." The following letter is addressed to a brother philosopher, who, like the gieut Tae- Foong himself, boasts that he and his successors for ten generations belore him have worn no tails þÿ a boast which implies that they have appeared in public with the flowing robes and venerable beards ot the descendants of Conlucius. " To my FltlENU ClIINQ Vano, SUKNAMED THE riULOSOl'IIEE." " Sweet, oh my friend, to the heart of the wanderer, are thoughts that look towaid his

home, and dear are the recollections of tho loved ones fie lias left. The land ol the stranger is lovely, pleasant are its fountains and fragrant its flowers, but those fountains muimur not so sweetly, those flowers are not so lair, as those of his native land. So speak I often, communing with myself as 1 wander among the barburiaus, an exile from the scenes of my youth. Gieat was my jov, friend of my soul ! when 1 heard the mariners' cry of "land' for I was wearied with the daily scenes ot the vessel and even the Ocean itself with its hurricanes and its calms, like a volume often read, tailed longer to interest me. " The vast domains of America are gov. eined by the puissant Emperor Foik. to whose gracious permission we doubtless owe our unquestioned passuge among the extensive fortifications and grinning batteries which guard this great city of New þÿYork. And now light the pipe, my friend, and settle thyself comfortably in thv choir, in that postuie which is best for grave reflection, !<>r greatly shall 1 marvel il thou findt-st not in this epistle much whereon to speculate "Our arrival excited a prodigious sensation among these simple minded people, anil with the love of novelty and excitement which is so common to all barbarians, they came in crowds to the shore to receive us. Greatly did they admire our vessel, and in truth a beautiful contrast did she present to their own all shapen and awkward craft beside her: but the tails of the seamen especially surprised them and many were their

ejaculations of astonishment on beholding them. " On landing we were received by a numerous and honorable body guard consisting of persons of all ages and sixes and of all degrees of filth. This peculiar cicorl, dciunni-
S'l,

P.attd in ihe language of the country " black, guards," is, as I am told, provided by the authorities oT the city whenever a distinguished guest arrives, and is Considered a mark of high respect. These irregular troops have a singular mode of saluting iturse whom they conduct ; it consists 'in placing the thumb of the right hand upon the nose, and then spreading the fingers apart, it reminded me strongly of a custom which 1 once noticed among the Tartars. " Thus attended and receiving fiom time to time these courteous salutations, which I. id course, on each occasion, acknowledged w ith & bow, we proceeded up the great street of the 'city, which we found inhabited bv vast herds of swine. These creatures when annoyed by any rash passengers exhibit tininislakeabte signs of ferocity, and I conclude that this animal is sacred heie, jnst as ihe bull is worshipped in various parts of >!e East. By the beard of my father ! 'tis sad to see a nation so sunk in ignorance and error. "So hemmed in was ! bv the crowd that could see but little of the city, as I passu along, except the streets, arid indeed the bogs of Tefan are as nothing in comparison. After long reflection I have come to the conclusion that they are purposely left in this fihhy stale in order to form burrowing places for the sacred swine. " Having with great difficulty Waded across the largest and filthiest of these si reels, we reached at last a great castle standing in the midst ol an open square, and here I was told the chief mandarin of the place awaited

my coming. Presently forth he stepped and immediately, according to the custom of the country, commenced a long oration, of which of course understood not a word; however, I smoked mv pipe in si'ence and from time to time gravely nodded my head to show him how entiieiy I coincided with him in all his opinions, and when we had concluded, 1 addressed to him a few remarks in the chaste and beautiful language of Chusan, which, however, 1 fear he comprehended as little as 1 did his English. The Portuguese fiist imported negro slaves from Western Africa into Eutope in 1442. Spain soon engaged in the traffic, and negro slaves abounded in some places ot that kingdom. After America was discover eil. the Indians of Hispaniola were impoited into Spain and made slaves. The Spaniards visited the coast of North America, and kidnapped thousands of the Indians, whom they transported into slavery in Europe and the West Indies. Columbus himself enslaved five hundred native Americans, and sent them into Spain, that they might be publicly soid at Seville. The practice of selling North American Indians into foieigh bondage continued nearly for two centuries. Negro slavery was first introduced into America bv Spanish slaveholders, who emigrated with their negroes A royal edict of Spam authorised negro slavery in America in 1508, King Ferdinand himself sent from Seville fifty slaves, to labour in the mines In 1511, the direct traffic in slaves between Africa and Hispaniola was enjoyed bv a royal ordinance Las Casas, who bad seen the Indians vanish away like dew before the cruellies of the Spaniards, suggested the

In 1507 anutiter expedition was piepared, and Queen Elizabeth protected and shared in the traffic. þÿ Hawkins, in one of his expeditions, set tiie to an African city, and out ol eight thousand inhabitants, succeeded iu seizing two hundred and sixty. Janies Smith ol Boston, and Thomas Keyser, first brought upon the colonies the guilt of participating in African slave tiade. In 1615 they imported a cargo of negroes from Africa. Throughout Massachusetts the cry of justice was raised against them as malefactors and murderers; the guilty men were committed for the offence, and the representatives of the people ordered the negroes to be restored to their native coumrv at the public charge. Liberia extends from Digby, at the mouth of the Poor River, on the north west, to Cavully River on the south east, between 4 deg. 20 min. and 6 deg 40 min. north latitude, and 7 deg. 30 min. and 1 1 deg. west longitude from Greenwich. The length of coast between Digby and the Cavally River is about three hundred miles. Inwards, the territory of Liberia extends from twenty to thirty miles. The right of possession and jurisdiction over the greater part of ibis hue has been purchased by the American and the Maryland Colonization Societies. The inhabitants ol Liberia, emigrants from the United States and their children number three thousand two hundred ; of whom seven hundred occupy the Maryland Colony at Cape Palmas To these may be added about five hundred natives, civilized and admitted to the privileges of the polls and the rights of citizenship in general. The natives residing on land owned by the colony, and directly amenable to its laws, are estimated at from 10,060 to 15.000. Permit me through the medium of thy (aaper to make known the result of an editing's opportunity, which on the 15ih July, it was my rich piivilege so enjoy, in ihe itch examination of various celestial objects With the gigantic equatorial telescope recently erected in the new observatory al Cantbridge. It is known to the public generally that for several years past piepaiations have been in progress at Cambridge, for the mounting of this noble instrument, which, during the same period, has been in course ol construction at Munich, in Germany, in view of the immense pains and cost involved, it was au interesting and fearful question whether its performance would equal the anticipation so long and anxiously indulged by the parties interested ; and belore speaking of this it may be useful briefly to advert to some of its properties, though a far more extended and scientific description of it will doubtless be prepared by the able director of lite observatory, William C. Bond, and ultimately published by the committee of examination. The pier on which it rests is of masonry, consisting of blocks of granite. It is a Lustrum of a cone, 20 feet in diameter at its base and ten at the top, and about 40 feel in height ; its base, however, is twenty feet below the surface of the ground. On us flat of granite, thirteen tons in weight, handsome- and level lop is placed the pedestal, to wi ich the telescope is attached, ft is a huge block 1

ly wrought, and of a construction adapted to the equatorial apparatus, consisting of ponderous masses of brass, and weighing, with the tube, certainly not less than tour tons: and yet so ingeniously and perfectly is friction evaded, that the merest child can give it motion and direct it to any point in the heavens. The object-glass of the instrument is fifteen inches in diameter in the clear; its focal length is 23 feet, and the length of the instrument, including the sliding tube, about 24 feet. That the reader may not deceive himself by comparing these dimensions with those of the telescope constructed by Sir William Herschell, or the greater one more recenily made by Lord tlosse, be may be reminded that these are reflecting telescopes, with metallic mirrors, and for equal duty, with the exception of what is termed space penetrating power, must greatly exceed in size. þÿ Sullice it to say, then, that the telescope at Cambridge is of the refracting kind, its optical duiies being performed by lenses; and to obtain a lense of filieen inches in diameter, of a sufficient purity to represent the object in perfect shape and color, under high magnifying powers, is an art of inconceivable dillieuliy. and at present, I believe, lias never been successfully accomplished by any other establishment than the one in which this telescope was manufactured. The secret was imparted by the lamented Fraunhofler, and so fearfully tenacious are they of the minutiae of the movements, that it is said they arc
unwilling to use any other poker to stir the melted mass than that which was employed by that illustrious man. No larger refract ing telescope has ever been iu successful operation iu the world.

!t is of corresponding size with the boasted instrument at the imperial obsei vatory at I'ulkova, maiiuhie.tured at (lie same establish inent ; but the Cambridge b-us is warranted lo be a< good, and by the maker believed to be better. This was also t lie opinion of Simms, the celebrated manufacturer ol Ln gland, who Was employed to inspect the lenses, side by side. The immense labor necessary in mounting and adjusting tin instrument of this construction and magnitude, without previous practice or experience, was greatly diminished by those preparations which the skill and ingenuity of the director enabled him lo effect, while the instrument and its various equipments wete in Germany; but the period since its arrival has not yet been sufficient to ten ier the adjustment perfect, nor is it at present preieuded to be fully prepared for use. To counteract the apparent diurnal motion of the celestial objects, which is continu ally throwing them out of the field ol ordinary telescopes, (a gieat annoyance, especially when high powers are employed.) a clock wotk is attached to the equatorial axis, so constructed as to give to the instrument a quiet and steady sidereal motion, contrary to the motion of the earth, which by a slight modification may tie applied to the solar or lunar motion ; hut it is generally sufficient when adjusted to a star. The effect of this arrangement is to keep the object lor several bouts constantly in the contie ol the field of view The night of the 15th was by no means a

favorable one. With the exception of scattering cirii, it was cloudless, hut the atmosphere was smokv, as it had been for the previous fortnight. The first object to which, at my request, the telescope was directed, was the planet Venus, invisible lo the naked eve, it being yet day light. The instrument was, however, adjusted to the right ascension and declination of the planet, and the clock work set in motion, when the object made its appearance in the centre of the field, and although veiled with smoke, and obscured by day light, it met the eye with a glare. What will be the effect ol a view ol ibis planet, in the absence of twilight, in a clear, autumnal evening, can only he imagined. The planet was only fourteen degrees from the horizon The intervening dense atmosphere of the earth, the mist and vapor always existing so near its surface, all magnified bv the instrument, were not sufficient to prevent a rich display of its disc, half illuminated, and much resembling the moon at the quarter, except a dusky hue, which I attributed to the dense atmosphere ol the planet. The view exceeded any idea that ! had entertained of the performance of the instrument ; but our opportunity was abridged by the necessity ol catching a glimpse at the moon, still nearer the horizon, and already veiling herself with cirri. The first object on the lunar surface that met my eye was the yawning gulf Endvmion, wide, deep and dark ; the line of illumination lea perl from each side, leaving a

frightful gap between The mountains generally stood out in hold relief, easting shadows black as midnight ; indeed, the entire length of the line dividing the light from the dark hemisphere exhibited a mass of ruin of unspeakable magnificence. The clock work was hardly adjusted when the mini set þÿ Notwithstanding me brevity of thcoppoitu

$ 3i D Jt rt AT a 3, " þÿ þÿ tiity ami the obscurity of the moon, 1 satisfied myself of the existence of the grey light spoken of by Sehrc.eter, indicating a twilight only compatible with the existence of a lunar atmosphere; a far more favorable opportune ty is probably near at hand, and this mooted question will he set at rest. At a later period of the evening our attention was directed to test objects. On a previous evening, the double star. Gamma Cororise, had been well separated with a power of 720. The mere separation of this star is thought to have been the highest attainment ol Prof. Strove, with the imperial instrument, but it was divided by the Gumhridge instrument without effort. This star was examin ed in 1832, by Sir J. Herschell, with his twenty leet reflector, when he only saw a round disc without a companion. The point of faint light, also, near Alpha Gapiieorin, which President Smyth says long baffled his rest arches, was boldiy exhibited by the Cambridge instrument. Sir John Herschell was led to suppose that this object was seen by reflected light þÿ a field of investigation which will not be likely to escape the attention of the Cambridge observeis. The companion of Antares, though obscured by haze and smoke, was very conspicuous. Sir J. Herschell, while at the Cape of Good Hope, could not have missed it for a moment, if he had turned his telescope upon it. inas much as it may be detected, under favorable circumstances, in this latitude, by a five feet equatorial. The telescope was now directed to the

close double star, Eta Coronre Close, indeed, it has been of late years, having set at defiance most of the telescopes in the world. It was at one time a lest object for telescopes, hut it has been recently closed. It nevertheless yielded to our power at once, and the dark thread which separated it could not have measured more than one third of a second. The instrument was next adjusted to the annular nebula between Beta and Gamma, in the constellation of the Lyre, and the clock work being applied, an opportunity was afforded me which I had often craved for a deliberate survey of an object whichi with smaller and less powerful instruments, had deeply interested me. With ordinary instruments, it appears to be a ring or wieath of stars, being entirely vacant in the centre, not ui. like what we might suppose to be the appearance of the Milky Way, viewed as a whole at an immense distance. Seen through the Cambridge telescope, it is no longer a ring, its centre is no longer dark, but filled with a multitude of small faint stars. Lord llosse's powerful reflector represented the interior as nebulous, a circumstance of which I was not aware when at Cambridge, and hence did not speak ot its resolvability, but i am ijuite sure the individual stars, (hough faint, were distinctly seen. The double star, 01 Cvgni, now engaged our attention: thus honored, only on account of the tank it holds in the history of science, being memorable for the researches of Besscl, lo whom it revealed its parallax. 1 was

struck, however, with the small, neat, round disc of the individual stars, giving additional evidence to that alicady obtained from their annual motion, that, distant as they may be bv our means and modes of measurement, these bodies are conipatalively near.

Search was now made for the double headed shot, or dumb bell nebula. i,s it is called, situated in the Fox's breast. I he instrument was set to its position, and it appeuied in the field. The director had scarcely applied his eye to the telescope before he expressed the opinion that the nebula was þÿlesoLed. The assistant observer was then called upon to examine it. and repeatedly said "it is resolved " I then applied mv own eye, and fouud it lo consist ot closely packed hut of individual stars. 1 am thus minute because this has been uniformly numbered among the irresolvable nebula;. It was first discoveted by Messier, many years since, and desCiibed bv hint as an oval nebula without a star. þÿ The Earl of Kosse, as we are mlormed by the president of tiie Astronomical Society of London, applied his powerful reflector to this object, and went so far as to say that "it exhibited symptoms of resolvabiliiy": but he did not resolv it ; nor am 1 aware that it has ever before yielded to the power of the telescope. The next object of scrutiny was the delightful cluster in Hercules 1 his was a sort of desert to the þÿentertainment, the sweetmeat of the feast. Well might Prof. Nicho! say that "no plate can give a fitting representation of it," and well might he add that " no one ever saw it for the first time through a telescope, without uttering a shout of 'wonder : hut i am sure that il the profi ssor were once to see it himself through the Gambridge instrument, his astonishment would

he unutterable. No new feature was exhibited, but its beauty and brilliancy were greatly magnified. The beautiful star Alpha Lyra; had now reached the meridian, and, from its high Northern declination, was much above the mist of the atmosphere. Willi this we were to take our leave of " these life infusing suns of other worlds" When the telescope was adjusted to this star, such was its dazzling brightness, and so thickly was surrounded by telescopic companions, that the assistant astronomer shouted when it met his eye. The powers employed on this occasion ranged from 250 to 750. The instrument is furnished with eye pieces magnifying two thousand times, Among the results which may be anticipated from this capital instrument, is the detection of plane's revolving about the fixed stars, which are strongly indicated by those faint points of white light, or minute stars, which cluster about Alpha Lyrre, of which i counted 23, and the sharper eye of the assistant observer numbered 35. Constant measurements of these, with high powers, will, it may he confidently expected, at no distant day make known the motions and laws of these wonderfully remote and complicated systems. WM.
